candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale' turned the individual question 'was someone like this person in the trial?' into a population comparison of two age distributions, and 'mapping' suggested laying one over the other.
candidates.working_title: The age of the trial and the age of the patients
candidates.core_insight: People in treatment trials have often been much younger than the people who have the condition, so before applying a trial result to an older person, look at the ages of the people who were studied.
candidates.angle: Put the two age distributions side by side. In a large analysis of US cancer treatment trials, a quarter of participants were 65 or over, while nearly two thirds of people with cancer were; heart failure trials showed the same pattern. The gap is visible in any trial's baseline table if you look for it.
candidates.position: A trial result applies most securely to people like those studied; for older people who were rare in a trial, the result is an extrapolation to be weighed, not assumed.
claims_needing_evidence: In 164 Southwest Oncology Group cancer treatment trials (1993 to 1996), 25% of participants were aged 65 or over, compared with 63% of US patients with cancer; in breast cancer trials the figures were 9% and 49% (Hutchins 1999, NEJM; abstract read).

Participants in heart failure trials published 1985 to 1999 were younger, more often male and more often had reduced ejection fraction than people with heart failure in the community, with no improvement over time (Heiat 2002, Arch Intern Med; abstract read; mean ages to extract from full text).
More recent analyses find the age gap between cancer trial participants and the cancer population persists (cohort or registry analysis, e.g. Ludmir 2019).
Trial reports give participants' age as a mean or median with a spread in the baseline table (CONSORT guidance).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Examine a neglected consequence', with 'averages' from the draw, led to the consequence of writing each guideline for an average person with one disease: the combined plan for someone who has several.
candidates.working_title: Several good guidelines, one person
candidates.core_insight: Following each single-condition guideline for a person with several conditions adds up to a plan that no trial tested and no guideline weighed as a whole, so the combined plan needs its own review.
candidates.angle: Each guideline is reasonable alone. Applied together to one hypothetical 79-year-old woman with five common conditions, US guidelines produced 12 medicines and a complicated non-drug regimen. A UK analysis found 133 potentially serious interactions between drugs recommended in the NICE type 2 diabetes guideline and drugs recommended in guidelines for 11 other conditions, few of them flagged.
candidates.position: For a person with several long-term conditions, the treatment plan should be reviewed as one plan against the person's priorities; adding up single-disease recommendations without that review is poor practice.
claims_needing_evidence: Applying guidelines for five common conditions to a hypothetical 79-year-old woman would lead to 12 medications and a complicated non-drug regimen, and most guidelines did not discuss applicability to older people with several conditions (Boyd 2005, JAMA; abstract read; daily dose count to confirm in full text).

Drugs recommended in the NICE type 2 diabetes guideline had 133 potentially serious drug-drug interactions with drugs recommended in guidelines for 11 other conditions (89 for depression, 111 for heart failure), and few were highlighted (Dumbreck 2015, BMJ; abstract read).
Applying five NICE guidelines to two hypothetical patients produced a considerable treatment burden and a complex follow-up and self-care regimen (Hughes 2013, Age Ageing; abstract read).
NICE guideline NG56 on multimorbidity recommends an approach that takes account of treatment burden and the person's priorities (official guideline; to open).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Reverse the default assumption' applied to research consent: the default of excluding adults who can't consent, reversed to including them unless the protocol gives a reason.
candidates.working_title: Exclusion should need a reason
candidates.core_insight: Many studies exclude people who can't consent for themselves by default, although UK law allows them to take part with safeguards, so people with conditions such as dementia and stroke end up with the weakest evidence for their care.
candidates.angle: The protective instinct to exclude produces a different harm: no evidence for the people most likely to receive the treatment. In two years of original research in a leading geriatrics journal, at least 29% of studies explicitly excluded people with cognitive impairment and only 6% justified it. Reversing the default means a protocol has to justify exclusion, using legal routes for inclusion that already exist.
candidates.position: Ethical judgement, stated as such: studies of conditions common in later life should include adults who lack capacity, with the legal safeguards, unless the protocol gives a scientific reason not to; exclusion by habit is unfair to them.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 434 original research articles in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society in 2008 and 2009, at least 29% used explicit exclusion criteria for cognitive impairment, 6% gave any justification and 14% discussed exclusion as a limitation (Taylor 2012, JAGS; abstract read; confirm denominators in full text).

Of 80 recently completed UK trials in conditions commonly associated with cognitive impairment, 15 included adults who lacked capacity to consent (Shepherd 2019, Trials; abstract read; confirm how the 80 were selected).

In England and Wales, the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (sections 30 to 34) allows research involving adults who lack capacity with ethics approval and a consultee's advice; in Scotland, the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 section 51 sets conditions including consent from a guardian, welfare attorney or nearest relative; trials of medicines follow the Medicines for Human Use (Clinical Trials) Regulations 2004, with a legal representative (legislation; to open).
The INCLUDE Impaired Capacity to Consent Framework gives trial teams questions and worksheets for designing inclusive trials (Shepherd 2024, Trials; abstract read).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Reverse the default assumption' with the draw's 'noise': the default that a change in a score is a change in the person, reversed to asking first whether the change is larger than the test's own variation.
candidates.working_title: Is the change bigger than the test's variation?
candidates.core_insight: Repeated measurements such as memory test scores and eGFR vary from test to test when nothing has changed, so a small change should be compared with the test's known variation and read with the history and daily function before it changes a diagnosis or a plan.
candidates.angle: In cognitively normal people aged 75 and over retested every 18 months, the MMSE had to change by 2 to 4 points before the change was reliable. Kidney guidance defines a 'certain drop' in eGFR as a fall in category plus a fall of at least 25%. Both are rules for telling a real change from variation, and neither replaces what the family reports.
candidates.position: A single small change in a test score is weak evidence of decline; act on changes larger than the test's variation, on a repeated trend, or on reported changes in daily life.
claims_needing_evidence: In 119 cognitively normal people aged 75 and over, tested six times at 1.5-year intervals, a change of at least 2 to 4 MMSE points indicated reliable change at the 90% level; small changes may reflect measurement error, regression to the mean or practice (Hensel 2007, JNNP; abstract read).
KDIGO 2012 defines a certain drop in eGFR as a drop in GFR category accompanied by a 25% or greater drop from baseline (KDIGO guideline; to open; check whether the 2024 guideline keeps this wording).
Dementia assessment includes informant history of change in daily function (NICE NG97; official guideline).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Count something nobody counts' became counting the exclusion criteria that remove older people from trials without naming any age.
candidates.working_title: Excluded without an age limit
candidates.core_insight: Trials often shut out older people without an upper age limit, through criteria such as other illnesses, several medicines, reduced kidney function, cognitive impairment, living in a care home or being unable to attend visits, so reading the whole exclusion list shows who a result can apply to.
candidates.angle: Upper age limits are the visible part. In ongoing heart failure trials, a quarter had an arbitrary upper age limit, but 43% had at least one poorly justified criterion that could indirectly keep older people out. A later review of recruitment found exclusion criteria, mainly age and other conditions, were the commonest reason for poor recruitment of older people.
candidates.position: When a trial's exclusion criteria remove many of the people most likely to receive a treatment, the report should say so, and readers should count those criteria before applying the result.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 251 ongoing heart failure trials registered in 2008, 25.5% excluded patients by an arbitrary upper age limit and 43.4% had one or more poorly justified exclusion criteria that could limit inclusion of older people (Cherubini 2011, Arch Intern Med; abstract read).
In a systematic review of 50 studies, exclusion criteria (mainly age and comorbidities) were the most common cause of poor recruitment of older adults (Forsat 2020, JAGS; abstract read).
Many 2020 COVID-19 treatment and vaccine trials had upper age limits or criteria likely to exclude older adults (Helfand 2020, JAMA Intern Med; research letter; figures to extract from full text).
Trials of drugs for common chronic conditions often exclude people with other conditions (systematic review, e.g. He 2020 or Buffel du Vaure 2016).

candidates.stimulus_use: The occupational therapist viewpoint, with 'count something nobody counts', pointed to what a person actually does on an ordinary day at home, which function scores rarely record.
candidates.working_title: Can do, did do, does do
candidates.core_insight: What a person says they can do, what they manage in a test and what they actually do on an ordinary day are three different measurements that often disagree, so any function score should say which one it records.
candidates.angle: A 1998 analysis called these the 'tenses' of function and found consistent disagreement between what older people said they could do and what they actually did at home. Discharge plans and trial outcomes often rest on one tense while the decision depends on another.
candidates.position: Assessments that inform discharge, care packages or research outcomes should state whether they record ability in a test or performance at home, and should include what the person does day to day.
claims_needing_evidence: Data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging showed consistent discordance between hypothetical function (what people say they are able to do) and enacted function (what they actually do at home) (Glass 1998, Gerontologist; abstract read).

The WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health distinguishes capacity (in a standard environment) from performance (in the person's usual environment) (WHO 2001; official).
Self-reported and performance-based measures of function in older people agree only moderately (review or validation study; to find).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' moved from the people in a trial to the people who were assessed and not included; the kitchen sieve suggested the screening funnel.
candidates.working_title: Read the first box of the flow diagram
candidates.core_insight: A trial's flow diagram reports how many people were assessed for eligibility and why they were not included, which tells a reader how selected the participants were, often the main limit on applying a result to older people.
candidates.angle: Readers go straight to the result. The first boxes of the CONSORT diagram describe the people the result may not apply to. In a review of trials in four major journals, only about half reported how many people were screened, and some screened as many as 68 people for each person enrolled.
candidates.position: Before applying a trial to an older person, read how many were assessed, how many excluded and why; a trial that doesn't report this leaves readers unable to judge how selected its participants were.
claims_needing_evidence: CONSORT flow diagrams report numbers assessed for eligibility, excluded with reasons, and randomised (CONSORT 2010 and CONSORT 2025 statements).

Of 172 RCTs in four high-impact journals (1999 to 2000), 52% reported the number of people screened for eligibility, and some trials screened as many as 68 people per person enrolled (Gross 2002, Ann Intern Med; abstract read).
A real trial in older people with a high ratio of screened to randomised participants, as a worked example (to find and verify; do not use until verified).

candidates.stimulus_use: The speech and language therapist viewpoint pointed to the consent process itself: information written for fluent readers screens out people with communication difficulties who could decide for themselves.
candidates.working_title: An information sheet only some people can read
candidates.core_insight: People with aphasia after a stroke are often left out of stroke research because consent materials assume fluent reading and speech, yet many can decide for themselves when information is given in an accessible form.
candidates.angle: The barrier is often the paperwork. In the trials included in a Cochrane review of information provision after stroke, 10 of 14 excluded people with aphasia and only one included them, though aphasia affects about a third of people after a stroke. Accessible information sheets and supported conversation are small changes that alter who takes part.
candidates.position: Research teams studying conditions that affect communication should provide accessible consent materials and communication support instead of excluding people who have difficulty reading or speaking.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 14 RCTs in a Cochrane review of information provision after stroke, 10 excluded people with aphasia, 1 included them and the rest did not report exclusion criteria (Brady 2013, Int J Stroke; abstract read).
About a third of people who have a stroke experience aphasia (Brady 2013 background; find the primary epidemiological source).
Aphasia does not in itself mean a person lacks capacity; capacity must be assessed with communication support (Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice; Brady 2013).
A structured consent support procedure helped include people with aphasia in consent (Jayes and Palmer 2014; to verify).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Ask who bears the cost' applied to taking part in research: travel, time and a companion's time fall on older participants and families; the service manager viewpoint suggested the budget line that could cover them.
candidates.working_title: Who pays for taking part
candidates.core_insight: Taking part in a study costs participants travel, time and often a companion's time, and designs that reduce these costs, such as home or remote visits, arranged transport and flexible appointments, help older people join and stay.
candidates.angle: Poor recruitment of older people is often put down to reluctance. A systematic review found the commonest barriers were exclusion criteria, families or doctors advising against taking part, lack of interest and transport, and that flexible teams and provided transport helped. Transport and flexibility are decisions made, and costed, at the design stage.
candidates.position: Trial budgets and protocols should cover the costs of taking part and fit visits to older participants; otherwise trials select the fittest and best-resourced older people.
claims_needing_evidence: In a systematic review of 50 studies, barriers to recruiting older people included exclusion criteria, families or physicians advising against participation (22% of studies), lack of interest (18%) and transport problems (18%); adapting recruitment methods (28%), a flexible team (26%) and provision of transport (24%) helped; flexible appointments and regular updates helped retention (Forsat 2020, JAGS; abstract read).
Missing data are more common in studies of older adults, and adapting data collection to the population's needs is a recommended prevention strategy (Hardy 2009, JAGS; abstract read).
UK guidance for inclusive trial design (STEP UP, building on NIHR INCLUDE) identifies funding, time and flexible protocols as facilitators (Biggs 2024, BMC Med Res Methodol; abstract read).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare what is recorded with what is experienced' set the medical record's disease count beside people's own rating of their health; the GP viewpoint suggested the problem list.
candidates.working_title: Several conditions, and health rated good
candidates.core_insight: In a large study of 85-year-olds in Newcastle, most had several diseases on record, yet about three in four rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age, so a list of diagnoses says little about how a person experiences their life.
candidates.angle: The problem list is what services count; self-rated health is what people report. The Newcastle 85+ Study measured both in the same people. Asking a person how they rate their own health gives information the record doesn't hold.
candidates.position: A long problem list shouldn't be read as a poor life; clinicians and families should ask the person how they rate their own health before assuming.
claims_needing_evidence: In the Newcastle 85+ Study (people born in 1921), women had a median of 5 diseases and men 4, and 77.6% (646 of 832) rated their health, compared with others of the same age, as good, very good or excellent (Collerton 2009, BMJ; abstract read). The post must keep the 'compared with others of the same age' wording.
The most common recorded conditions were high blood pressure and osteoarthritis, and hearing impairment was present in about 60% (Collerton 2009; abstract read).
evidence_leads: Collerton J et al. Health and disease in 85 year olds: baseline findings from the Newcastle 85+ cohort study. BMJ 2009;339:b4904. PMID 20028777, PMC2797051 (abstract checked on PubMed; full text available)

candidates.gain: A reason, and permission, to ask an older relative how they rate their own health.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Take a common shortcut and qualify it', with the trial designer and 'five years', pointed to the standard five-year risk estimate, which misleads when many people die of other causes first.
candidates.working_title: When five-year risk figures run high
candidates.core_insight: In older people, standard survival analysis can overstate the chance of an event such as a fracture because it treats people who died of something else as if they were still at risk; competing-risk methods give lower, more realistic figures.
candidates.angle: In the Framingham Osteoporosis Study, the usual method overestimated the 5-year risk of a second hip fracture by 37% and the 10-year risk by 75%, relative to a method that accounts for death. The error grows with age and length of follow-up, which is exactly where prevention decisions in later life are made.
candidates.position: Risk estimates used for decisions in older people should account for the competing risk of death; when a paper or tool doesn't, both the risk and the expected benefit of prevention are likely to be overstated.
claims_needing_evidence: Kaplan-Meier and Cox methods can overestimate disease risk in older populations by not accounting for the competing risk of death; in the Framingham Osteoporosis Study, survival analysis overestimated the 5-year risk of second hip fracture by 37% and the 10-year risk by 75% compared with competing-risk estimates (Berry 2010, JAGS; abstract read; absolute risks to extract from full text).
Cumulative incidence functions and Fine-Gray regression are standard competing-risk methods (methods review, Austin 2016).
FRAX accounts for the competing risk of death in its 10-year probabilities (FRAX methods paper; unsure; verify before mentioning).
evidence_leads: Berry SD, Ngo L, Samelson EJ, Kiel DP. Competing risk of death: an important consideration in studies of older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2010;58:783-7. PMID 20345862, PMC2873048 (abstract checked on PubMed; full text available)

Kanis JA et al. 2008, Osteoporos Int, FRAX methodology and mortality (unsure)

candidates.pause: Few clinicians know that the figure they quote may be inflated by the method.
candidates.gain: A question to ask of any risk figure used for a frail or very old person: did it allow for deaths from other causes?
candidates.follow: Reading the evidence posts here deal with the statistics that change decisions in later life.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none in the earlier collection. In the current set, C07-20 covers absolute benefit and living long enough to benefit; this is the statistical method that inflates the risk. C20-16 is a different problem (deaths removing people from later measurements).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the scale' moved from an age-group average to the spread of individuals within each age group; the doctor in training suggested the reader who uses age as a quick guide.
candidates.working_title: Age tells you less the older people get
candidates.core_insight: Differences in health between people of the same age tend to widen in later life, so a person's age is a weaker guide to their health, and to what a treatment will do for them, at 85 than it is in middle age.
candidates.angle: Group averages fall with age, but the range around them is wide. In US survey data, 28% of people aged 85 and over rated their health as excellent or very good, and 56% reported no health-related limit on work or housework. Averages describe the group; the decision is about the person.
candidates.position: Treatment and service decisions should rest on the person's health, function and goals; age alone becomes a poorer basis for decisions as people get older.
claims_needing_evidence: Of gerontological studies that reported measures of dispersion, 65% found variability increased with age, more so in longitudinal studies (Nelson and Dannefer 1992, Gerontologist; abstract read).

In US survey data, 28% of those aged 85 and over reported excellent or very good health and 56% reported no health-based limitations in work or housework; health-related quality of life ranged widely within every age group (Lowsky 2014, J Gerontol A; abstract read).
The WHO World report on ageing and health describes wide diversity in health and function in older age (WHO 2015; official).
evidence_leads: Nelson EA, Dannefer D. Aged heterogeneity: fact or fiction? Gerontologist 1992;32:17-23. PMID 1740251 (abstract checked on PubMed)
Lowsky DJ, Olshansky SJ, Bhattacharya J, Goldman DP. Heterogeneity in healthy aging. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2014;69:640-9. PMID 24249734, PMC4022100 (abstract checked on PubMed)
World Health Organization. World report on ageing and health. 2015
Beard JR et al. The World report on ageing and health: a policy framework for healthy ageing. Lancet 2016;387:2145-54
candidates.opening_line_draft: People differ more in health at 85 than at 50. That is why your age tells a doctor less about you than it seems.
candidates.visual_idea: Two parts. Top, labelled 'Illustrative example, not measured data': rows for ages 50, 70 and 90, each with dots spread along a line from 'poor health' to 'excellent health', the spread wider in older rows. Bottom: two simple bars with Lowsky's verified figures for people aged 85 and over. Source credit.
candidates.pause: It turns a familiar complaint about ageism into a measurable fact about variation.
candidates.gain: A plain reason to ask that decisions rest on your health and wishes, not your birth date.
candidates.follow: The account explains the evidence behind fair treatment of older people.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E023 (don't use age as a reason not to diagnose dementia) is a clinician instruction on one condition; this explains why age is a weak guide in general. In the current set, C17-06 (age a poor guide to loneliness) is one specific case.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' moved to the participant after a study ends; the envelope and 'order of events' suggested the results letter that often never comes.
candidates.working_title: Ask how you will hear what the study found
candidates.core_insight: If you are asked to take part in a research study, you can ask at the start how and when you will be told what it found, and UK research regulators expect researchers to tell participants the findings.
candidates.angle: People give their time to research and are often never told the outcome. Asking at the start makes it part of the plan. It sits with a few other questions that help older people decide: what taking part involves, whether visits can be at home, whether someone can come with you.
candidates.position: People who take part in research should be told the findings in a form they can use; asking for this at the start is reasonable and expected.
claims_needing_evidence: The Health Research Authority's 'Make it Public' strategy (2020) expects researchers to inform participants of study findings (official document; to open and confirm wording).
Most research participants say they want to receive study results (survey or review, e.g. Shalowitz and Miller 2008).
Many trials don't share results with participants (audit or survey of investigators, e.g. Raza 2020).
Participants can withdraw from a study at any time (HRA guidance on participant information).
evidence_leads: Health Research Authority. Make it Public: transparency and openness in health and social care research. 2020 (official; unsure of exact wording)
Shalowitz DI, Miller FG. Communicating the results of clinical research to participants. PLoS Med 2008;5:e91 (unsure)

candidates.opening_line_draft: Before you agree to take part in a research study, ask how and when you will hear what it found.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: the main question in large type, with three follow-up questions beneath ('What will taking part involve for me?', 'Can visits happen at home, and can someone come with me?', 'Can I stop at any time?'). A drawn older woman reading a letter at a kitchen table, clearly an illustration.
candidates.pause: Many older people have taken part in a study and never heard the result.
candidates.gain: Questions that give them more control over taking part.
candidates.follow: The account treats older people as partners in research, not only subjects of it.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Companion to C20-21 (registering for research); schedule apart.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' was applied to age thresholds: a service or study that starts at a fixed age meets people in the poorest areas later in their illness, because long-term conditions arrive earlier there.
candidates.working_title: Illness in later life arrives earlier in poorer areas
candidates.core_insight: In Scotland, people in the most deprived areas develop several long-term conditions 10 to 15 years earlier than people in the most affluent areas, so services and studies that use a fixed age as their entry point reach poorer people later in their illness.
candidates.angle: An age threshold looks neutral. Applied to populations whose health declines at different ages, it isn't: the same birthday marks different stages of illness in different postcodes. Eligibility based on need, such as frailty or function, reaches people when they need it.
candidates.position: Judgement: services and studies for older people shouldn't rely on age alone as the way in, because a fixed age reaches people in poorer areas later relative to their need.
claims_needing_evidence: In 1.75 million people registered with 314 Scottish practices (2007), onset of multimorbidity occurred 10 to 15 years earlier in people living in the most deprived areas than in the most affluent (Barnett 2012, Lancet; abstract read).

Healthy life expectancy differs by many years between the most and least deprived areas of Scotland and of England (NRS and ONS official statistics; figures to open and verify; official web pages may not open here, so a published paper quoting them may be needed).
The absolute number of people with multimorbidity was higher under 65 than over 65 (Barnett 2012; abstract read; supporting point only).

candidates.pause: The size of the gap, in years, surprises most readers.
candidates.gain: A concrete reason to judge services by need rather than birth date.
candidates.follow: The account pays attention to who is poorly served, with Scottish data.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none in the earlier collection. In the current set, C03-01 (hip fracture in poorer areas) and C17 poverty candidates concern outcomes; this concerns age thresholds.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare what is recorded with what is experienced', from a care home manager's viewpoint, pointed to the gap between what national data record about care homes and what residents experience.
candidates.working_title: What nobody counts in care homes
candidates.core_insight: England has no routine national minimum data set on care home residents, so their health, function and quality of life are largely missing from routine statistics; a national study has now built and piloted a prototype.
candidates.angle: Care homes are counted as beds, registrations and inspection ratings; the people in them are much less visible. The DACHA study linked care home records with NHS and social care data for over 700 residents and found that measures used in care home research were mostly clinical, with quality of life under-represented. The pandemic exposed the gap.
candidates.position: Residents' health and quality of life should be measured routinely, as they are for other groups of NHS patients; without it, the care of some of the most dependent people in the country is hard to judge or improve.
claims_needing_evidence: England lacks a care home minimum data set; the DACHA study developed and piloted a prototype linking care home records with NHS and social care data, with 727 residents' data included (Goodman 2026, Health Soc Care Deliv Res; abstract read).

Reviews within DACHA found measures used in care home research were mostly clinical, with under-representation of measures important to care homes such as quality of life (Goodman 2026; abstract read).
The lack of linked datasets for care homes hampered the response to COVID-19 (Hanratty 2020, BMJ editorial; to read).
Scotland collects some resident-level information through the Care Home Census for Adults (Public Health Scotland; official; check content so the England and Scotland difference is stated correctly).
US nursing homes certified by Medicare and Medicaid must complete Minimum Data Set assessments for residents (CMS; official; only if the comparison is used).

candidates.gain: Understanding why care home quality is so hard to compare, and what a minimum data set would change.
candidates.follow: The account keeps care homes and their residents in view.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none in the earlier collection. In the current set, C16 covers care in care homes and C08-13 covers dementia outcomes; this is national measurement.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Name the trade-off openly' became the trade-off in follow-up length: longer follow-up measures outcomes older people care about but loses more people, and those lost tend to be the sickest; 'inventory' suggested taking stock of who is still counted.
candidates.working_title: When the people who died drop out of the average
candidates.core_insight: In studies of older people, deaths and dropouts remove the sickest people from later measurements, so average function among those still measured can look better than the group's real course; check how deaths and missing data were handled.
candidates.angle: Longer follow-up is more relevant and more incomplete. Missing data are more common in ageing research because participants have more health and functional problems. Outcomes that count death alongside function, such as being alive and independent, avoid flattering the survivors.
candidates.position: Studies reporting function or quality of life in older people should report deaths and missing data alongside the result and use analyses that include them; readers should be wary of an improving average when many people are missing.
claims_needing_evidence: Missing data are more likely in studies of older adults because of health and functional problems; reports should disclose missing data and dropout rates and compare dropouts with completers (Hardy 2009, JAGS; abstract read).
When follow-up is truncated by death, the choice of analysis changes what an average among survivors means (Kurland 2009, Stat Sci).
Composite outcomes such as disability-free survival include death in the outcome (e.g. ASPREE, McNeil 2018, NEJM).
evidence_leads: Hardy SE, Allore H, Studenski SA. Missing data: a special challenge in aging research. J Am Geriatr Soc 2009;57:722-9. PMID 19220562, PMC2695652 (abstract checked on PubMed)
Kurland BF, Johnson LL, Egleston BL, Diehr PH. Longitudinal data with follow-up truncated by death: match the analysis method to research aims. Stat Sci 2009;24:211 (unsure of pages)
Diehr P, Johnson LL, Patrick DL, Psaty B. Methods for incorporating death into health-related variables in longitudinal studies. J Clin Epidemiol 2005 (unsure)
McNeil JJ et al. Effect of aspirin on disability-free survival in the healthy elderly. NEJM 2018;379:1499-508
candidates.opening_line_draft: If the sickest people in a study die before the 12-month assessment, the average at 12 months describes the people who were left.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram labelled 'Illustrative example, not real data': ten figures at the start, each with a function score; at 12 months three are marked as having died and one as missing; two summary boxes compare 'average of those still measured' with 'how many are alive and independent', showing how the first flatters the group.
candidates.pause: It explains why some studies of very old people report improving averages that don't match clinical experience.
candidates.gain: Two things to check in any study of function in later life: how many died or dropped out, and how they were counted.
candidates.follow: Reading the evidence posts here are specific to the problems of studying older people.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. In the current set, C07-05 reports ASPREE's disability-free survival result; this is the reading skill behind that kind of outcome. C20-11 covers a different problem (competing risk inflating event risk).

candidates.working_title: What would you advise if I were 20 years younger?
candidates.core_insight: Asking a clinician what they would advise if you were 20 years younger, and why, shows whether a recommendation rests on reasons about your health or only on your age.
candidates.angle: Sometimes the advice should differ with age: the benefit may take longer to arrive, or the risks may be higher with other conditions. Sometimes age is used as a shortcut. The question makes the reasoning visible without accusing anyone, and the answer is useful either way.
candidates.position: Age can justify different advice only through what it says about benefit and risk for the person; you are entitled to hear those reasons.
claims_needing_evidence: Age discrimination in the provision of services, including health and social care, has been unlawful in Great Britain since October 2012 unless it can be objectively justified (Equality Act 2010; official; confirm commencement date and exceptions).
Age-based differences in access to treatment are documented across many studies (systematic review, Chang 2020; WHO Global report on ageism 2021).
For some preventive treatments, the time before benefit appears can exceed a person's likely remaining life, a legitimate reason for different advice (time-to-benefit studies, e.g. Lee 2013 BMJ).
evidence_leads: Equality Act 2010, age provisions for services and public functions (commenced 1 October 2012; unsure of exact exceptions)
Chang ES, Kannoth S, Levy S, Wang SY, Lee JE, Levy BR. Global reach of ageism on older persons' health: a systematic review. PLoS One 2020;15:e0220857 (unsure of figures)
World Health Organization. Global report on ageism. 2021
Lee SJ et al. Time lag to benefit after screening for breast and colorectal cancer. BMJ 2013;346:e8441 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: When a treatment isn't offered, one question shows the reasoning: what would you advise if I were 20 years younger, and why?
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: the question in large type; beneath, two labelled boxes: 'Reasons about your health and goals' (how long any benefit takes; risks with your other conditions; what you want from treatment) and 'Reasons about the number alone'. Drawn older man speaking with a doctor at a desk, both seated at eye level.
candidates.pause: Older readers who have wondered whether age alone shaped a recommendation recognise the situation.
candidates.gain: One polite question that brings the real reasons into the open.
candidates.follow: The account gives older people and families words to use in real appointments.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E023 (don't use age as a reason not to diagnose dementia) is addressed to clinicians and one condition; this is a public question for any treatment. Check C07 treatment-decision candidates (time to benefit) for compatibility.

candidates.working_title: Healthy ageing can include illness
candidates.core_insight: The World Health Organization defines healthy ageing by what a person is able to do and be, which depends on their surroundings as well as their body, so a person with long-term conditions can still be ageing healthily, and changes to their surroundings can add to what they are able to do.
candidates.angle: Definitions that require the absence of disease leave out most older people: in a Californian study, 19% met such criteria while 50% rated themselves as ageing successfully, many of them with chronic conditions. WHO's functional definition counts the grab rail, the hearing aid, the bus route and the bench on the way to the shops as part of health.
candidates.position: Explanatory, with one judgement: an older person's health is better judged by what they can do and value than by their diagnoses, and improving their surroundings is part of improving it.
claims_needing_evidence: WHO defines healthy ageing as the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age; functional ability comprises a person's intrinsic capacity, their environment and the interactions between them (WHO 2015; Beard 2016, Lancet).

In 867 Alameda County Study participants aged 65 to 99, 50.3% rated themselves as ageing successfully, compared with 18.8% classified as successful by Rowe and Kahn's criteria; many with chronic conditions or functional difficulties rated themselves as ageing successfully (Strawbridge 2002, Gerontologist; abstract read).

Beard JR, Officer A, de Carvalho IA, et al. The World report on ageing and health: a policy framework for healthy ageing. Lancet 2016;387:2145-54
Strawbridge WJ, Wallhagen MI, Cohen RD. Successful aging and well-being: self-rated compared with Rowe and Kahn. Gerontologist 2002;42:727-33. PMID 12451153 (abstract checked on PubMed)
Rowe JW, Kahn RL. Successful aging. Gerontologist 1997;37:433-40
candidates.opening_line_draft: By the World Health Organization's definition, a person with arthritis, poor eyesight and heart failure can still be ageing healthily.

candidates.pause: It contradicts the idea that any diagnosis ends healthy ageing.
candidates.gain: A practical way to think about health that includes changes a family or council can make.
candidates.follow: The account explains ideas about ageing in plain, usable terms.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Distinct from C20-10 (self-rated health against disease counts); schedule apart if both are selected.

candidates.working_title: A clot test cut-off adjusted for age
candidates.core_insight: Because D-dimer rises with age, a fixed cut-off rules out pulmonary embolism in few older people; using age multiplied by 10 as the cut-off in people over 50 with a non-high clinical probability let far more people aged 75 and over avoid a scan, with no extra missed clots in that group.
candidates.angle: An example of a test made to work better for older people by evidence rather than assumption. In the ADJUST-PE study, among people 75 and over with non-high clinical probability, the share in whom pulmonary embolism could be excluded without imaging rose from 6% to 30%. It applies only after a clinical probability score.
candidates.position: Clinicians should know the age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off and consider it, as UK guidance allows, for people over 50 with a low or unlikely clinical probability of pulmonary embolism.
claims_needing_evidence: In ADJUST-PE (3346 outpatients with suspected pulmonary embolism), the age-adjusted cut-off was age x 10 in patients 50 or older; the 3-month failure rate among those with D-dimer above 500 but below their age-adjusted cut-off was 1 in 331 (0.3%); among 673 patients aged 75 or over with non-high clinical probability, exclusion without imaging rose from 43 (6.4%) to 200 (29.7%) with no additional false negatives (Righini 2014, JAMA; abstract read).
The rule is used only with a clinical probability assessment (Wells or revised Geneva score) (Righini 2014).
NICE NG158 advises considering an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold for people over 50 (official guideline; to open and confirm wording and units).
Units depend on the assay (µg/L fibrinogen equivalent units); the post must state the rule in the units the evidence used.

candidates.working_title: Told you have stage 3 kidney disease at 85?
candidates.core_insight: Many older people are told they have stage 3 chronic kidney disease after a routine blood test; in a large US study of people with this level of kidney function, those aged 85 and over were more likely to die of other causes than to need dialysis at every level studied, so asking whether the result is stable, what the urine test shows and which medicines need a different dose is more useful than fearing dialysis.
candidates.angle: The label worries people, and the useful information is usually in three follow-up questions. Kidney risk is judged by eGFR together with albumin in the urine, and a stable result without albumin carries a low risk of kidney failure. The label still has uses: some medicines need a lower dose, and heart and blood pressure care may change.
candidates.position: Explanatory, with a practical instruction: an older person given a stage 3 kidney disease result should ask whether it is stable, what the urine albumin test shows and which medicines need a dose change.
claims_needing_evidence: In 209,622 US veterans with CKD stages 3 to 5, older patients had higher rates of death and lower rates of end-stage kidney disease than younger patients at comparable eGFR; among those 85 and over, the risk of death always exceeded the risk of end-stage kidney disease (O'Hare 2007, JASN; abstract read). The sample was mostly men; state that it is a US veterans study.
KDIGO grades CKD risk by both eGFR and urine albumin categories, and risk is lower where albumin is normal (KDIGO 2024; official).
NICE NG203 recommends measuring urine albumin to creatinine ratio alongside eGFR (official; to open).
Some medicines need dose adjustment according to kidney function (BNF; see C06-19 for the Cockcroft-Gault point).
Whether CKD should be defined differently by age is debated (Delanaye 2019); the post should take no side.

candidates.follow: The account explains test results without false alarm or false reassurance.

candidates.working_title: You can volunteer for health research
candidates.core_insight: Older people are under-represented in research that concerns them, and in the UK anyone can register to be contacted about studies, through SHARE in Scotland, Join Dementia Research across the UK and the NIHR's Be Part of Research service.
candidates.angle: Much of the exclusion happens before anyone is asked. Registers work the other way round: the person says they are willing, and researchers come looking. Registering doesn't commit anyone to a study.
candidates.position: Explanatory: registering is a practical way for older people and carers to be asked about studies, and it doesn't oblige them to take part.
claims_needing_evidence: SHARE, the Scottish Health Research Register run by NHS Research Scotland, lets people register interest in research and allows their health records to be used to match them to studies (official; confirm current operation and age eligibility).
Join Dementia Research, run by NIHR with charity partners, lets people with and without dementia, and carers, register interest in dementia studies across the UK (official; confirm).
Be Part of Research is the NIHR service for finding UK studies (official; confirm scope in Scotland).
Registering does not commit a person to take part in any study (each service's terms; confirm).
Older people are under-represented in many trials (Hutchins 1999; Cherubini 2011).

candidates.gain: A concrete action for older people who want research to include people like them.
candidates.follow: The account turns criticism of exclusion into something readers can do.

candidates.working_title: Checking the 7.5 years
candidates.core_insight: The often-quoted finding that people with positive views of their own ageing lived 7.5 years longer comes from one observational cohort of 660 people; later pooled studies support a small link, but the figure describes an association, and reverse causation and confounding remain possible.
candidates.angle: The number is used to argue against ageism, which deserves better support than an overstated statistic. A meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found a small but significant effect of views of ageing on health and survival, strongest with shorter follow-up. The case against ageist treatment is ethical and needs no survival figure.
candidates.position: Quote the 7.5-year figure only with its limits; the argument against ageist treatment rests on equal dignity, not on a single observational estimate.
claims_needing_evidence: In 660 people aged 50 and over in the Ohio Longitudinal Study of Aging and Retirement, those with more positive self-perceptions of ageing, measured up to 23 years earlier, lived 7.5 years longer, after adjustment for age, gender, socioeconomic status, loneliness and functional health (Levy 2002, JPSP; abstract read).

A meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found a small significant effect of subjective ageing on health, health behaviours and survival, with stronger effects for shorter follow-up and younger samples (Westerhof 2014, Psychol Aging; abstract read).
Observational associations can reflect reverse causation (people in poorer health may view ageing more negatively) and residual confounding (general methods point; state as interpretation).
evidence_leads: Levy BR, Slade MD, Kunkel SR, Kasl SV. Longevity increased by positive self-perceptions of aging. J Pers Soc Psychol 2002;83:261-70. PMID 12150226 (abstract checked on PubMed)

World Health Organization. Global report on ageism. 2021 (check whether it cites the 7.5-year figure; unsure)

candidates.visual_idea: Annotated statement card: the figure in large type as a quoted claim, with three labelled notes: 'One cohort, 660 people, Ohio', 'Observational: shows a link, not a cause', 'Pooled studies: a smaller effect'. Source credits.
candidates.pause: Many readers have shared the figure; few know where it came from.
candidates.gain: An honest way to use the finding, and a firmer basis for the argument against ageism.
candidates.follow: The account is sceptical of overclaiming even when the claim supports a cause it holds.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Others rate older patients' lives lower than the patients do
candidates.core_insight: In studies of older outpatients and of hospital patients aged 80 and over, doctors and family surrogates judged the patients' quality of life or health values lower than the patients themselves did, so a treatment decision that brings in quality of life should start by asking the person.
candidates.angle: Doctors' estimates of older outpatients' quality of life were linked with the doctors' own views on life-sustaining treatment, while the patients' own ratings weren't linked with their treatment preferences. In a US study of hospital patients aged 80 and over, most were unwilling to trade much time for excellent health, and less willing than their surrogates assumed.
candidates.position: Clinicians should ask older patients how they rate their own quality of life before using it in any treatment decision; estimates made on their behalf tend to run low.
claims_needing_evidence: Primary physicians (n=105) rated 258 chronically ill older outpatients' global quality of life, physical comfort, mobility, depression, anxiety and family relationships significantly worse than the patients did; physicians' estimates were associated with their attitudes to life-sustaining treatment, while patients' perceived quality of life was not associated with their own preferences (Uhlmann and Pearlman 1991, Arch Intern Med; abstract read).

Of 414 hospitalised patients aged 80 and over, 68.6% would give up at most 1 month of 12 in exchange for excellent health; patients traded significantly less time than surrogates assumed, and 20.3% of surrogates underestimated by 3 months or more (Tsevat 1998, JAMA; abstract read).
Both are US studies from the 1990s; a more recent replication would strengthen the post (to search).
evidence_leads: Uhlmann RF, Pearlman RA. Perceived quality of life and preferences for life-sustaining treatment in older adults. Arch Intern Med 1991;151:495-7. PMID 2001131 (abstract checked on PubMed)
Tsevat J et al. Health values of hospitalized patients 80 years or older. JAMA 1998;279:371-5. PMID 9459470 (abstract checked on PubMed)
A recent study comparing clinician and patient ratings of quality of life in older adults (to search; unsure whether a strong one exists)

candidates.pause: Clinicians who believe they judge quality of life fairly are confronted with evidence that they don't.
candidates.gain: A simple rule for any conversation about treatment intensity.
candidates.follow: The account questions clinical habits with evidence, including clinicians' own.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E129 (a good frailty conversation includes what the person still wants) is related; this adds evidence that others' estimates run low. candidates.working_title: Measure the goal the person set
candidates.core_insight: Goal attainment scaling measures progress on goals the older person chooses, each scored from much worse to much better than expected, and in a trial of geriatric assessment it detected meaningful change that standard function and quality-of-life scales missed.
candidates.angle: Standard scales measure what every patient is assumed to want. In a Canadian trial of a mobile geriatric assessment team for 265 frail older people in rural areas, goal attainment scaling was the most responsive measure and the only one to detect clinically important change.
candidates.position: Services and trials in geriatric medicine should measure outcomes against the person's own goals as well as standard scales; goal attainment scaling is one tested way to do it.
claims_needing_evidence: In an RCT of an interdisciplinary Mobile Geriatric Assessment Team in 265 rural frail older adults, goal attainment scaling was the most responsive measure at 3 months, compared with the Barthel Index, Physical Self-Maintenance Scale, IADL and a quality-of-life index, and only goal attainment scaling detected clinically important change (Rockwood 2003, J Clin Epidemiol; abstract read).
Goal attainment scaling scores each goal on a five-point scale from -2 to +2, with 0 as the expected outcome (Kiresuk and Sherman 1968).
evidence_leads: Rockwood K, Howlett S, Stadnyk K, Carver D, Powell C, Stolee P. Responsiveness of goal attainment scaling in a randomized controlled trial of comprehensive geriatric assessment. J Clin Epidemiol 2003;56:736-43. PMID 12954465 (abstract checked on PubMed)

candidates.visual_idea: Diagram labelled 'Illustrative example': one goal ('Walk to the corner shop and back') with its five levels written out from -2 to +2, the expected level highlighted, and a tick at the level reached at review.
candidates.pause: It suggests some good geriatric care has looked ineffective because the wrong thing was measured.
candidates.gain: A tested method a team can start using in clinic or rehabilitation.
candidates.follow: Care that works posts give methods, not slogans.

candidates.working_title: The words used about an ageing population
candidates.core_insight: In a US experiment, short messages that presented ageing in terms of older people's contributions, accumulated experience, or how age prejudice works reduced measured age bias in readers, while a plain message about ageing did not, so the words chosen to describe an ageing population can change attitudes.
candidates.angle: Talk of an ageing population as a crisis casts longer lives as a problem to be managed. The experiment was a single session measuring implicit bias, so the effect is modest and its duration unknown. Writers about care can still choose to describe needs and solutions, and to name the people.
candidates.position: Judgement: people writing about care and services should describe an ageing population in terms of needs, contributions and solutions rather than catastrophe; framing research gives this modest support.
claims_needing_evidence: In a nationally representative US sample (N=767), participants randomised to one of three framed messages about ageing showed lower implicit age bias on an implicit association test than controls; an unframed message about ageing did not differ from control (Busso 2019, J Gerontol B; abstract read).
Catastrophe framing of population ageing is common in media coverage (media content analysis; to find, or drop this claim).
WHO's Global report on ageism describes ageism as widespread and harmful and identifies interventions (WHO 2021; official).

candidates.gain: Specific wording choices for reports, bids and posts.
candidates.follow: The account applies evidence to how health and care are talked about.

candidates.working_title: Reading the age subgroup in a forest plot
candidates.core_insight: When a trial reports that its effect was consistent across age subgroups, the oldest subgroup may hold few people and have a wide confidence interval, and a non-significant test for interaction is weak evidence that the effect is the same in them.
candidates.angle: Subgroup analyses have little statistical power, so 'no significant difference between subgroups' is easily read as 'works just as well at 85'. Check the number of people and events in the oldest subgroup, the width of its interval, where the top age cut-off sits (65 or 75 can hide the over-85s), and the absolute risks.
candidates.position: A non-significant age interaction is not proof of equal benefit in the oldest; trials should report the oldest groups with numbers and absolute effects.
claims_needing_evidence: Tests of interaction have low power; detecting an interaction as large as the overall effect needs about four times the sample size (Brookes 2004, J Clin Epidemiol; to verify the figure).
Guidance on reporting and interpreting subgroup analyses (Wang 2007, NEJM; Sun 2010, BMJ).
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence (Altman and Bland 1995, BMJ).
Trials often use 65 or over, or 75 or over, as the top age subgroup (to verify with named examples such as SPRINT's 75 and over).

candidates.gain: Four checks to apply to any age subgroup.
candidates.follow: Teaching rounds here make statistics usable at the bedside.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none. Public counterpart is C20-27.

candidates.working_title: When the evidence stops before your age
candidates.core_insight: When a treatment was studied only in younger people, the lack of evidence at older ages is a gap, which is different from evidence that it fails; the decision then rests on how the treatment works, its known risks at older ages, how long any benefit takes and what the person wants.
candidates.angle: The same phrase, 'there's no evidence at your age', covers two situations. One question separates them: was it tested in people like me and found not to help, or was it not tested in people like me? Each answer leads to a different conversation, sometimes to a trial of treatment with a planned review.
candidates.position: An evidence gap should lead to a weighed decision, sometimes a time-limited trial of treatment, rather than automatic refusal or automatic prescribing.
claims_needing_evidence: Older people, especially those over 80, are under-represented in many trials (Hutchins 1999; Heiat 2002; Cherubini 2011; abstracts read).
Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence (Altman and Bland 1995, BMJ).
The risks of some treatments rise with age and frailty (name specific, sourced examples when drafting, e.g. bleeding with anticoagulants or falls with sedatives).
Time to benefit is a recognised consideration in prescribing for older people (Holmes 2006, Arch Intern Med).

candidates.follow: Weighing it up posts help people through real treatment decisions.

candidates.working_title: An outcome set built for older people
candidates.core_insight: An international consensus set of outcome measures for older people's health care lists what services should track, including taking part in decisions, autonomy, mood, loneliness, pain, daily activities, falls, time in hospital, strain on carers and place of death, and a service can compare its own measures against it.
candidates.angle: Most services report activity such as admissions, length of stay and waiting times. The ICHOM set was designed for health care providers and those who pay for care, not for researchers, and it starts from the person's experience. Laying a service's dashboard beside it shows what is missing.
candidates.position: Services for older people should measure some outcomes from this set, especially taking part in decisions, loneliness and place of death, which activity data miss.
claims_needing_evidence: The ICHOM standard set for older persons recommends: participation in decision making, autonomy and control, mood and emotional health, loneliness and isolation, pain, activities of daily living, frailty, time spent in hospital, overall survival, carer burden, polypharmacy, falls and place of death; it was developed by modified Delphi and intended for health care providers and payers rather than research (Akpan 2018, BMC Geriatr; abstract read). In the post, 'carer burden' should be described as strain on carers.
Routine NHS performance reporting is largely activity-based (admissions, length of stay, waiting times) (official statistics; phrase generally and check).

ICHOM Older Person standard set reference guide (official; unsure of current version)

candidates.working_title: Three kinds of 'we don't know'
candidates.core_insight: Clinical uncertainty comes in different kinds, such as known odds of several outcomes, missing evidence for people like this patient, and several conditions interacting unpredictably, and naming which one applies helps an older person and their family understand what, if anything, could reduce it.
candidates.angle: 'It's uncertain' is often said as if it were one thing. A published taxonomy separates uncertainty from probability, from ambiguity (missing or conflicting evidence, common for older people because of trial exclusion) and from complexity. Each calls for a different response: a number, an honest statement of the gap, or a trial of treatment with review.
candidates.position: When telling an older person that an outcome is uncertain, clinicians should say which kind of uncertainty it is and what would reduce it.
claims_needing_evidence: Han, Klein and Arora proposed a taxonomy of uncertainty in health care with sources including probability, ambiguity and complexity (Med Decis Making 2011; verify category names).
Evidence on how best to communicate uncertainty to patients is limited (review, Simpkin and Armstrong 2019; verify).
Older people are under-represented in trials, creating ambiguity for decisions about them (Cherubini 2011; Hutchins 1999; abstracts read).

candidates.follow: The account treats uncertainty as something to explain, not to hide.

candidates.working_title: Talking therapy works in later life
candidates.core_insight: In NHS psychological therapy services in England, people aged 65 and over were more likely than working-age adults to recover and less likely to drop out, yet older people are under-represented among those treated, so an older person with depression or anxiety should be offered, or ask about, talking therapy.
candidates.angle: Assuming low mood is a natural part of ageing, or that older people don't take to therapy, keeps them out of services where their outcomes are better. In more than 100,000 patients across eight services, older adults had higher adjusted odds of reliable recovery, with the usual cautions of an observational study.
candidates.position: Depression and anxiety in later life should be treated as treatable, and older people should be offered psychological therapy on the same terms as younger adults.
claims_needing_evidence: In more than 100,000 patients in eight Improving Access to Psychological Therapies services, older adults (65 and over) were more likely to reliably recover and reliably improve, and less likely to drop out, than working-age adults after adjustment; possible selection bias and residual confounding are acknowledged (Saunders 2021, J Affect Disord; abstract read). For the public, give crude recovery percentages by age group from the full text rather than odds ratios.
Older adults are under-represented in psychological treatment services (Saunders 2021 background; find the primary source, e.g. NHS Digital annual IAPT or Talking Therapies report).
In England, people can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies; arrangements in Scotland differ (official; confirm).
